title: A Warm and Koji Thanksgiving: Miso Caramel Apple Tarte Tatin
contentHtml:
A touch of white miso paste adds savory complexity to the buttery, flaky, caramel flavors of a traditional French tarte Tatin.

Combining butter and koji—whether in a creamy miso Beurre Blanc, used to roast vegetables, combined in toffee, or used to churn koji-fermented cream into funky and complex koji butter—is a flavor combination rabbit hole that I’ve yet to find the bottom of. The fun part is that the flavors of koji (the Japanese mold responsible for the flavor of miso paste and soy sauce) are naturally both savory and sweet, which means that koji-fermented products can work really well in both savory and sweet applications.

Adding miso to a tarte Tatin (a French upside-down apple tart built around buttery caramel) seemed like a natural move and an easy way to get a crowd-pleasing apple dessert on the Thanksgiving table with minimal fuss.

There’s not much to it: I cook sugar and water into a light amber caramel then add butter and white miso paste. The miso adds salt along with a little fermented complexity that gives the caramel more depth. It’s not an Earth-shattering change. The apples still taste like apples, the caramel still tastes like caramel, the pastry still tastes like pastry, but your tongue stops for a second when you take a bite and asks your brain, “Wait, what makes this taste so good?”

Some Apples Can’t Take the Heat

For tarte Tatin, you want apples that soften without turning to apple sauce. My apple pie testing over the years has taught me that a crisp raw apple doesn’t necessarily make a good cooked apple. Pectin (the carbohydrate glue that helps hold vegetable cells together) breaks down as apples cook. Acidity helps slow that breakdown—which is why tart apples tend to hold their shape better as they cook—while the density of the apple can also affect how well it keeps its shape.

Golden Delicious or Granny Smith are my first choice, closely followed by Gala and some modern varieties like Honeycrisp.

Avoid, at all costs, the Red Delicious. It’s a mealy, flavorless apple designed by people who hate apples, schoolchildren, and joy.

I use store-bought puff pastry for mine. You could make your own blitz puff pastry, or use a simple pie dough like my Easy Pie Dough, but I rarely have the patience to make my pastry from scratch. 

Once you flip the tart, the pastry ends up underneath a glossy layer of caramelized apples with the lightly salty, deeply savory flavor of miso.

Or at least it should. If one, like me, decided to eyeball the caramel instead of measuring—even when you're following your own darn recipe—one may end up with a tart that's not quite as glossy as one likes.

I tend to undershoot with the caramel, worried that making too much will cause the crust to go soggy, though in all honesty, this has never happened to me. Instead, I get a tart that's delicious, but lacks the shiny caramel coating of a properly sticky tarte Tatin.

This is why bakers tend to measure things, I suppose.

If you want to take the koji love a step further, you could pair the tarte Tatin with a bit of Koji-Fermented Whipped Cream by adding a few tablespoons of dry koji grains to a cup of heavy whipping cream and letting it rest on the counter overnight. The next day, strain the grains out and whip the cream with a tablespoon of sugar until it forms stiff peaks. Serve dollops of it on top the the tart, letting the koji-fermented cream melt into the miso caramel as you eat.

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • White miso adds salty, savory depth to buttery caramel, and everything comes together in a single skillet before getting topped with pastry and baked.

  • Pairs perfectly with Koji Whipped Cream—doubling down on our "Warm and Koji" theme and adding more savory–sweet complexity.

Yield: Serves 6 to 8
Active Time: About 30 minutes
Total Time: About 1 hour 45 minutes, plus pastry thawing

Notes:

  • Use a 10-inch oven-safe nonstick skillet or well-seasoned cast iron skillet. Golden Delicious apples are my preference; Gala also work. Choose firm apples weighing about 6 to 7 ounces (170 to 200 g) each.

  • Store-bought puff pastry, homemade blitz puff pastry, or enough Easy Pie Dough for one single-crust pie will work. Keep the pastry cold until ready to use.

  • Miso makes the butter-sugar mixture darker from the outset, so watch for a light caramel aroma as well as a change in color. Keep the heat moderate to avoid scorching it.

Ingredients

  • All-purpose flour, for dusting

  • 1 sheet store-bought puff pastry, thawed but cold, or dough for one single-crust pie

  • 4 tablespoons (55 g) unsalted butter

  • 1 tablespoon (about 18 g) white miso

  • ¾ cup (150 g) sugar

  • 5 Golden Delicious or Gala apples, peeled, quartered, and cored

  • Vanilla ice cream and/or Koji Whipped Cream, for serving

Method

  1. Prepare the pastry. Adjust an oven rack to the middle position and preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). On a lightly floured counter, roll the pastry into a 10-inch circle about ⅛ inch thick. Transfer to a plate, cut three small slits in the center, and refrigerate.

  2. Make the miso caramel. Melt the butter in a 10-inch oven-safe skillet over medium–low heat. Stir in the miso until evenly distributed, then add the sugar. Cook, stirring gently and adjusting the heat as needed, until the sugar melts and the mixture begins to caramelize lightly. It may look grainy or separated along the way. Stop at a light amber color and gently toasted aroma; it will continue to darken as the apples cook.

  3. Add the apples. Remove the skillet from the heat. Carefully arrange the apple quarters on their sides in a snug ring around the edge, then fill the center with the remaining pieces. The caramel is hot and may sputter as you add the fruit.

  4. Cook down the juices. Return the skillet to medium–low heat, cover, and cook until the apples release their juices, 10 to 15 minutes. Uncover and continue cooking until the juices reduce to a syrup, about 5 to 10 minutes longer, adjusting the heat to prevent scorching. Gently shake the skillet occasionally and spoon some of the caramel over the apples. Remove from the heat.

  5. Top and bake. Lay the chilled pastry over the apples, gently tucking its edges inside the skillet. Bake until the pastry is deeply golden and cooked through and thick caramel bubbles around the edges, about 50 minutes to 1 hour.

  6. Rest and invert. Let the tart rest for 20 to 30 minutes. Loosen the edges with a thin spatula, then place a large rimmed serving plate upside down over the skillet. Wearing oven mitts, hold the plate and skillet firmly together and carefully invert. Lift off the skillet and replace any apples that have stuck. Serve warm with vanilla ice cream and/or Koji Whipped Cream.
